INSIDE THE MODEL

A small model. Every assumption visible.

For each world, Parallel gives both options the same economic conditions, spending shocks and employment-shock draws. Each option responds according to its own salary, costs and risk assumptions.

Next savings = current savings + take-home pay − rent − living costs − transport − unexpected bills

What the numbers mean

“Finishes ahead”
The fraction of paired worlds where London ends with more savings, or a higher time-adjusted score when a time value is set. Exact ties are counted separately.
Expected regret
The average gap between choosing an option now and the better option in hindsight in each world. It is measured in pounds of the selected score, not emotional regret.
Rent tipping point
The London base rent where the average score of the two choices is equal. It uses the same simulated rent growth and shocks; it is not the rent where London wins exactly 50% of worlds.
Middle 80%
The 10th–90th percentiles of savings at each month. This is a pointwise range, not a guarantee that 80% of entire paths stay inside the band.
Monte Carlo error
A sampling error estimate will appear after a run.
Limits
Illustrative inputs, no live rental or labour-market data. Costs are nominal GBP. No interest, debt costs, taxes beyond the take-home input, asset returns, household changes or non-financial career value are modelled. Shared shocks assume strong positive dependence. Results depend on this choice.
YOUR ASSUMPTIONS

Open the black box.

Every input below is an example, not a researched estimate. Take-home pay is already after tax.

Shared assumptions: annual inflation varies by world (SD 1.5 percentage points); rent growth adds SD 2.5 points. Wage-growth SD is 2.5 points. A shared 3% monthly bill risk costs £300–£1,500. Unemployment pays an assumed 20% fallback income. All shocks are shared across options; the job-loss thresholds can differ.
A TWO-MINUTE WALKTHROUGH

Show the decision changing.

  1. Start with the offer. London pays £850 more each month. The model includes higher rent, moving costs and employment risk.
  2. Ask “Show me the downside.” Look at the worst-decile savings and the chance of crossing the £5,000 buffer.
  3. Ask “What would change my mind?” The tipping point gives you a concrete question to take to a landlord.
  4. Ask “Lower London rent by £200.” The agent changes one assumption and re-runs the same worlds.
  5. Set a value for your time. The commute preference can change the time-adjusted comparison while the cash chart stays separate.
  6. Export the run. Every input, seed, result and tool action can be inspected and reproduced.

Built as a simulated Alexa+ experience. No live Alexa+ account or Amazon credentials are required.
